title: Build a job search agent
description: A system that turns a job posting into a tailored application packet, a tracker entry, and an honest list of gaps.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

airtable.title: Airtable
airtable.content: A spreadsheet-database hybrid for tracking structured data — projects, content calendars, CRMs, inventories. Often used as the storage layer behind AI workflows because it has a clean API and connects to every major automation tool.

database.title: Database
database.content: An organized place to store and retrieve data — like a spreadsheet on steroids. When Claude builds an app that remembers users or saves entries, it's reading from and writing to a database (often Supabase or Postgres).

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: The average job opening now draws around 242 applications, per [The Interview Guys' State of Job Search research](https://blog.theinterviewguys.com/the-average-job-opening-now-gets-242-applications/), which makes mass-applying with one resume a volume game no one wins by hand. This system turns a posting into a tailored application packet and a logged pipeline entry with a follow-up date, in one pass per posting.

Tailoring materials to the actual posting is what moves reply rates. It pulls the requirements a posting emphasizes and maps each to real experience you already have, so nothing gets invented and no near-miss requirement gets quietly skipped.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) per posting, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill) triggered from your job board tabs, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that checks feeds and queues matches for your review. Every version stops short of pressing submit.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming the roles and locations you're targeting, where it watches for postings, what your resume needs to emphasize per role type, and how applications get tracked.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that runs my job search for me. Ask me questions, one at a time, about the roles and locations I'm targeting, where it should watch for postings, what my resume needs to emphasize per role type, and how I want applications tracked. When you have what you need, write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to state your targeting criteria before any posting gets judged against them, so matches stay consistent instead of a gut call per posting.

items: Where postings come from, since not every job board is scrapeable.
Where the tracker lives and whether it checks for duplicates before logging a new entry.
How much tailoring runs automatically versus waiting on your review.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are a spreadsheet or [database](#tooltip-database) for the tracker (Google Sheets, [Notion](#tooltip-notion), [Airtable](#tooltip-airtable)), the job boards you're watching (LinkedIn, Indeed, company sites), and email for drafts and digests (Gmail, Outlook). The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real posting. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn a job posting into a tailored application packet and a tracker entry.

Context: [Paste the posting. Paste or reference a file with your experience. Note the role type and level you're targeting.]

Rules:
- Pull the 3 to 5 requirements the posting emphasizes and map each to a real line from my experience. Never invent experience.
- Draft a cover letter under 250 words addressing those requirements.
- Flag any requirement I clearly don't meet.
- Log the company, role, date applied, and a follow-up date 7 days out.
- Output as a Requirement Match table, a Cover Letter Draft, and a Tracker Row.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: mapping each requirement to a real line from your own experience keeps the cover letter honest instead of confident-sounding fiction.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every requirement mapped to real experience, letter under the word limit, gaps flagged instead of glossed over?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what's off ("too generic on requirement 2, tie it to the actual metric") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Connect job boards through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) and schedule a weekly digest of new matches.
Have it build an interview-prep brief from the tracker once a company responds.
Track reply rate by resume version.
Add a duplicate check against postings already logged.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) your AI chat drafts, so quality isn't just a gut call. Have it draft a run log in the same pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each application packet, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, company, requirements matched, requirements flagged as gaps, and reply received. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the guesswork on whether a cover letter addressed the posting, and the log makes reply rate visible across resume versions after a few weeks of entries.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few weeks straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. It never submits anything for you, and it won't quietly cover for a requirement you don't meet. A wrong fact in a cover letter costs the role, so treat every flagged gap as real before you apply.
